title: Dell Is Finally Making Money On GenAI As Traditional Servers Boom
author: Timothy Prickett Morgan
text:
COMPUTE

Dell Is Finally Making Money On GenAI As Traditional Servers Boom

Timothy Prickett Morgan

Timothy Prickett
Morgan

Co-Editor, Co-Founder, The Next Platform

Published
wed 25 Nov 2026 // 15:58 UTC

Dell ended its third quarter of fiscal 2027 with $60.2 billion with new bookings for AI servers, a backlog of these machines of $132.3 billion, and a pipeline of new orders that is many times as large as this. By Dell’s historical standards, this is absolutely ginormous. Until you realize that Dell, the largest supplier of server machinery in the world in terms of revenues and probably shipments thanks to the GenAI boom, is a mere fraction of the $2.5 trillion “cloud industry backlog” that Nvidia revealed it had when it talked about its latest financials last week.Presumably the total Nvidia backlog, which includes demand from AI model makers, enterprises, governments, and academic institutions, is even larger than $2.5 trillion. But it is probably not larger than $3 trillion to $3.5 trillion, if I have to put a number on it.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

Despite all of the crazy amount of money being promised for future spending on the GenAI boom, Dell is only getting a piece of the action that is proportional to its share in systems and storage overall. The good news is that Dell is getting better and better at building immense AI clusters based on Nvidia technology, and bragged in its call with Wall Street going over the Q3 F2027 numbers that it can move customers from cluster delivery to first tokens generated in a little over six hours because machines are preconfigured and pretested at the factory.This, in fact, is what is hard about scaling up production of AI clusters. You have to build a massive datacenter to test machines in the factory before you put the gear on a truck. Only a dozen companies in the world – be they original design manufacturers (ODMs) or original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) who act like ODMs sometimes – can do this at scale.But to make this all work, and result in an invoice generating event for Dell, there are some other important steps.“Behind every customer engagement and every order is a rigorous due diligence process, resulting in a fully vetted backlog,” Jeff Clarke, vice chairman and chief operating officer at Dell, explained on the call with Wall Street going over the numbers. “Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power. Each design is bespoke, optimized through multiple iterations with the customer. Through this tight collaboration, we know our customers well and have a high conviction that our backlog will convert to revenue.”

NEXTPLATFORM AD

This part of the process may be the most important of them all. Enthusiasm is easy in the age of GenAI. Getting the cash is the hard thing.Like many IT suppliers, whether they make chips or systems, Dell has largely become a company serving the datacenter thanks to the GenAI boom. This stands to reason given that GenAI has effectively doubled the size of the IT systems sector in a few short years with an entirely new computing architecture that organizations are pretty sure will result in more efficient operations and new revenue sources.

Dell has always sold various kinds of services, including tech support and financing. And back in the day when Dell was trying to emulate IBM (as was Hewlett Packard Enterprise), the company even acquired hosting and systems integration services that comprised a large portion of its overall enterprise revenue stream. But like HPE, Dell sold off these businesses many years ago to focus on the hardware business, and its product-services split reflects this.In the third quarter, Dell had just a tad over $6 billion in services, up a mere 4.6 percent year on year. Product sales, however, rose by 2.3X to $48.93 billion.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

Add it up, and across the datacenter and PC businesses, Dell brought in $54.94 billion in sales, more than double year on year. Operating income was up a very nice 3.5X to $7.44 billion, and net income rose even faster at 2.7X to $5.67 billion. That net income represented 10.3 percent of revenues, the highest level we have ever seen out of Dell in its modern incarnation, and it is reasonable given the boom in sales of traditional servers as well as in sales of AI clusters that are getting moderately more profitable that Dell will be able to increase its datacenter profit margins even more in the coming quarters.

Dell ended the quarter with $16.26 billion in cash and investments, up 43.5 percent, but the company’s debt pile also grew by 20.7 percent to $37.7 billion.Dell’s Infrastructure Solutions Group datacenter business, which sells servers, storage, switching, and services for this gear, now represents more than three quarters of the company’s total revenue.

In Q3 F2027, sales of servers and networking drove a bit over $37 billion in revenues, up 3.65X year on year and up 37.5 percent sequentially from Q2 F2027. Storage revenues rose by a much more normal – if anything can be said to be normal these days – 23.8 percent to $4.93 billion. But here’s the very good news that Wall Street may not be paying attention to as I write this because the market is in the midst of a tech selloff: Operating income for ISG was up by 4.1X year on year to $7.12 billion, which represents 17 percent of revenues.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

By contrast, the Client Solutions Group, which sells PCs, laptops, workstations, and gaming machines, had $12.89 billion in sales, up 3.3 percent, and operating income was a mere $704 million, down 5.9 percent and representing only 5.5 percent of revenues.

Sales of AI servers did better than expected in Q3 F2027 than Dell had expected. Guidance for the quarter was for around $19 billion in revenues for AI servers, but it actually came in a smidgen north of $22 billion, which represented 3.9X growth year on year. The backlog for AI servers, as we said, was very strong at $132.3 billion, up by a factor of 7.2X compared to this time last year, and bookings in Q3 F2027 were up 4.9X year on year with that $60.2 billion level I mentioned at the top of this story.Dell says that it now has more than 7,500 customers of its AI servers, an increase of 1,000 customers since Q2 F2027. 

Don’t get the wrong idea, though. The traditional server business is growing like gangbusters, too. Part of that is due to the need for agentic AI sandbox systems – where AI tasks actually get performed – to complement AI inference systems that process inputs and figure out what tasks to do. But part of the reason traditional sales are rising faster and reaching higher than anything we have seen in four decades – including the Dot Com boom, by the way – is because there is a lot of relatively ancient server iron out there in the enterprise, government, and service provider datacenters of the world, and even with higher CPU, DRAM, and flash prices for core-laden systems, an economic argument can be made for getting rid of this older iron to free up datacenter space and electricity for other important things, and importantly AI inference.This is an unexpected bonus for the ODMs and OEMs of the world.By the way, in that chart above, the server share is shown for the X86 server market only and ignores the increasing fleets of Arm-based servers that the hyperscalers and cloud builders are deploying based on their own chip and system designs.

Dell’s storage business is plugging along, but it is eating share as well as Dell is growing faster than its peers even if that growth is nowhere near as large as seen with AI and traditional servers.
